abstract: Background: Genetic variants in the de novo DNA methyltransferase DNMT3A increase inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) risk, yet the mechanisms linking defective DNMT3A to IBD remain unclear. As macrophages gatekeep immune homeostasis, we characterized how myeloid-specific DNMT3A loss affects monocytic differentiation and inflammatory properties. Methods: We generated myeloid-specific Dnmt3a-deficient mice (Dnmt3a-LysM) via LysM-cre. Deletion was confirmed in gut lamina propria CD11b+ cells and bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDM). M1/M2-polarized BMDMs were characterized by methylation profiling, mRNA-sequencing, flow cytometry, arginase/NOS activity, phagocytosis (FITC-zymosan), and co-culture with wounded ModeK epithelial monolayers. Colitis was induced using dextran sodium sulfate (DSS). Results: Dnmt3a expression was induced by M2 and repressed by inflammatory stimuli in wild-type (Dnmt3afl/fl) BMDMs. Upon IL-4/IL-13 stimulation, Dnmt3a-LysM BMDMs exhibited heightened ERK1/2 and PI3K signaling, reduced M2 markers, increased pro-inflammatory Irg1/Tnf transcripts, and acquired M1-like features; amplified in BMDMs from aged (>34 weeks) mice (disrupted morphology, enhanced phagocytosis, reduced arginase and elevated iNOS activity). These cells impaired epithelial regeneration in co-culture. In vivo, young Dnmt3a-LysM mice showed splenic immune alterations and DSS-colitis hypersensitivity. Aged Dnmt3a-LysM mice displayed altered bone marrow architecture, hepatosplenomegaly, and myeloproliferation. Conclusions: Dnmt3a is required for physiological macrophage polarization. Its myeloid-specific loss drives pro-inflammatory skewing, potentially contributing to IBD pathogenesis.
